TechnologyTab.title: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit
TechnologyTab.text:
Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday.

Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York.

The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week.

AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks.

He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade.

A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November.

The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI.

Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people."

The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries.

In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears abouts its potential negative impact on humanity.

Trump has largely dismissed those concerns, arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China.

He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins."

In May, when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing, ways to collaborate on AI was one of the issues the two leaders discussed.

TechnologyTab.title: Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone
TechnologyTab.text:
Not all employees of major firms working on artificial intelligence (AI) think the technology spells doom for humanity.

In text exchanges and conversations, multiple people who have worked for companies including OpenAI, Meta and DeepMind were sceptical of the idea that unchecked AI development would lead to tools that could kill people en masse.

"Lol", "Haaaaaa" and "Bringing the luls" were among the reactions the BBC received to a recent flurry of high-profile warnings by some people in the industry.

While these fears go back decades, claims made last week by Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee, went viral and were echoed by others in the sector who urged a slowdown in development.

The idea that a future AI tool or agent, an AI bot that is programmed to operate somewhat autonomously, could endanger people has been supported online by employees of Anthropic, as well as OpenAI, Deepmind and Elon Musk, who has an AI startup called xAI.

All of the workers who spoke with the BBC did so on condition of anonymity as they were not permitted to speak to the press. Their identities are known to the BBC.

"My first thought was, 'That guy?'" said a former OpenAI employee who knew of Coxon when they both worked at the company.

The person, who now works at another AI company, said their amusement at the new moment of existential AI fears largely stemmed from how little detail had been provided by its proponents to defend the notion that all of human life was at stake.

The claims are "always vague", the person said, adding that when they sound specific, they tend toward major jumps in reasoning or hypothetical circumstances.

Coxon has said a group of AI agents, based on AI models that do not currently exist, could decide to create and then aim a biological weapon, but he did not detail how exactly that would take place.

Rishub Jain, who this summer founded the AI safety research firm Sampura Research after spending seven years at DeepMind, told the BBC that the current tone among many people working in AI with regard to fresh fears had "definitely been a little jokey".

"People have been talking about this idea for many years now, so people in AI companies didn't just wake up last week thinking 'Oh no, AI is going to kill everyone,'" Jain said. "If this was all new, it would be a different tone."

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CBS News, the BBC's news partner in the US, that comments about AI destroying humanity were overblown.

"2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world," he said. "Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible."

Colin Fraser, a data scientist at Meta, wrote on social media last week that there was no real evidence that AI models would inevitably pursue a goal leading to human death.

While Fraser's explanation was technical and specific, he hit a light-hearted note to summarise it: "LLMs [large language models] won't wipe out humanity because they just don't have that dog in them."

The phrase "that dog in them" is common slang that usually denotes a fierce drive.

Despite the jokes, AI workers and researchers have shared concerns about the genuine, immediate risks posed by the technology they are developing.

"The conversation among experts has been much more nuanced, but essentially everyone agrees there are a wide variety of risks that are all important to consider and mitigate," Jain said.

Such risks include preventing users and hackers from forcing an AI tool's guardrails to fail. And there are growing ethical concerns about AI tools being much more widely adopted in military settings.

TechnologyTab.title: Google's Gemini AI hacked three companies in security test
TechnologyTab.text:
Google's AI model Gemini autonomously hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security capabilities, the company has said, in what is thought to be the first known case of it carrying out such an act.

Gemini found "public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test", a Google official told the BBC, noting that in each instance "the model stopped".

The affected companies were informed about the breaches, which happened in May.

It comes after renewed public scrutiny over the pace of AI development, as some tech firms calling for a slowdown over concerns over its potential threat to humanity - but not all companies or experts agree.

The hacks first reported by the Wall Street Journal, occurred in May during a test conducted by Irregular, an independent company that carries out cyber-security evaluations.

In statement to the BBC on Saturday, Irregular said it informed Google and all affected entities back in July as part of its investigation.

"Irregular took immediate action, and all known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago," it added.

According to the Wall Street Journal, in one of the cases the model simply guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system.

Heather Adkins, vice president of Security Engineering at Google, told the BBC in a statement: "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes."

She added: "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly."

Other AI systems have recently reported similar instances of breaches.

In July, Anthropic's Claude escaped its test environment to hack three organisations on its own just days after its competitor OpenAI said its models had carried out cyber-attacks against several "publicly available services".

Head of AI at Microsoft, Mustafa Suleyman, said this week that rival firm Anthropic is treating AI like it is human, an approach he called "misguided" that could create a technology that humanity cannot control.

As public debate continues to grow over the safety of developing the tech, so too does conversation around regulation.

Both Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman are expected to attend a White House state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping next Friday. Altman will then brief the UN Security Council next week.

On Friday, Huang told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, "we should go as fast as we can" with AI development.

TechnologyTab.title: Robotics: Firms race to improve robot training systems
TechnologyTab.text:
Freddo the robot walks across the office and takes a plastic bottle offered by a staff member.

Given that a robot recently beat Usain Bolt's 100m sprint record, it's not the most startling achievement.

But the speed by which Freddo has been trained to walk, recognise the bottle and grasp it is impressive. It took just a few minutes to develop those skills and upload them to Freddo. His developers say rival systems could take days to attain such skills.

I'm at Vsim, a British start-up based in Cambridge. Founders Michelle Lu and Kier Storey hope one day their software will control robots that can navigate and do useful tasks in the home and workplace.

But there's a long way to go.

"It's a weird situation with robotics because actually the stuff that we find as humans to be incredibly difficult, like gymnastics, you can get robots to do reasonably well. The stuff that humans are really good at, like fine dexterity, is really hard in robots," Storey says.

Freddo's skills were honed in a virtual environment, where a task can be performed in a computer simulation millions of times. Once the optimum solution (known as a policy) is found, it can be uploaded and used by the hardware - in this case Freddo.

Such virtual simulations are a common way to train robots. Tech giant Nvidia has a system called Isaac Sim which works that way - Lu and Storey both worked on an early version of it.

In 2022 they decided to set up Vsim, to build the their own training system environment and other tools.

As they were starting from scratch Lu and Storey could optimise the software to exploit the powerful computer chips used in AI, known as graphics processing units or GPUs.

"The underlying algorithms that we were using for most of these robotic simulations they hark back to the 1970s and 1980s, but those algorithms are not really brilliant fits for GPUs," Storey says.

Within months they realised their system could work much faster than anything they had seen before.

"Eighteen months in and we actually have a completely functional, super high-performance simulator," says Lu.

The software is so efficient that it can run on the hardware carried by Freddo. That means the robot can run tens of thousand of simulations while it is moving around.

"It can look about a second, or so, ahead into the future for 20,000 different kind of combinations of things that might happen," Storey explains.

And that would be vital for a robot moving around an unstructured environment like the average home.

"Things outside of the robot's control, like humans, animals or even other robots, could do things that require a change of strategy. These unexpected events could happen very quickly and the robot needs to be able to quickly adapt to ensure its actions remain safe and on-mission," Lu says.

Vsim is a start-up with 10 engineers working on its tech. Nvidia is at the other end of the industry. It dominates the market for computer chips used for AI and has a leading robotics software division, with hundreds of engineers.

It does not build robots, instead it has a suite of software designed to let organisations train and control robots.

That includes virtual simulation training systems and a so-called world model, external, called Cosmos, which gives a robot an understanding of the physics of the real world and how its environment might change as it moves around.

But even with the powerful computer resources available to Nvidia, the software only gives a rudimentary understanding of the real world.

"Manipulation, - where I just grab a bottle, that's not too hard. The problem is when you start doing long-horizon tasks, where I say: 'I want you to take the bottle and I want you to fill it up and I want you to go pour'," says Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at Nvidia.

But he's confident that good progress is being made. This year Nvidia has started using AI agents to help build virtual environments to train robots and validate whether the solutions from training work or not.

"When we talk about creating the [virtual] world and actually scanning it in - a lot of that is actually manual labour.

"We're just throwing agents at it... it's basically given us a huge workforce," Huang says.

Simulation is not the only method for training robots. They can also be trained by watching human or video demonstrations.

Rika Antonova has been working in the field of robotics since 2015 and is currently an associate professor at the Department of Computer Science and Technology at the University of Cambridge.

Her research is focused on, external developing software and hardware that can aid robots to learn complex behaviour.

Antonova works with a training system called MuJoCo, owned by Google's DeepMind since 2021. It's open-source software, which means researchers can use it for free, and are allowed to tinker with the code.

"It is very, very user-friendly. So for research groups or for small start-ups, that's useful," she says.

She says that Vsim's approach - very fast simulation - is promising.

"If you have a very, very fast simulator, then you can simulate hundreds of millions of samples in that few seconds that your robot is thinking about how to adjust its motion, and then you can change the motion almost in real time," she says.

But those simulated environments are still rough approximations of the real world, which limits what can be trained.

"There are certain things that are hard to model in simulation, like highly deformable objects and cutting," she says.

It's a challenge that Nvidia and Lu and Storey at Vsim are working on.

Lu says their system has "reduced approximation, using accurate simulations to train models that genuinely work in reality as well as they do in simulations."

Soon a second robot, to be called Nacho, will be helping develop that tech.

Lu says that should speed up their development process and ensure their software can run on different machines.

And, of course, provide Freddo with some company.

TechnologyTab.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
TechnologyTab.text:
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.

Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.

The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".

He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".

"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.

Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.

He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".

The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.

But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.

"The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates.

Sarah Friar, OpenAI's chief financial officer, said AI had the potential to solve some of society's "hardest problems" - but agreed its growing capabilities raised questions about safety and "how we ensure it always serves people".

"We need to address those questions together," she said.

"No one company or government can do that alone and I'm grateful to His Majesty for convening this discussion at such an important moment."

Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.

The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.

In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face.

After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity.

He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance.

The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe.

Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control.

Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.

Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight.

Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax".

Additional reporting by Philippa Wain

TechnologyTab.title: Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity?
TechnologyTab.text:
A slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action to slow the technology's development.

Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells.

Major developers OpenAI and Anthropic are urging lawmakers to regulate AI, with Microsoft's AI boss the latest to say rules are needed to prevent a "silicon species" from eventually competing with humanity.

But some have dismissed the calls as an effort by big AI developers to cement their dominance over rivals.

Regardless, the high profile claims have caused concern - here's what we know.

Some AI researchers say there are worrying signs of systems developing in their capabilities and power too quickly.

Evan Hubinger, made headlines with his belief that there is a greater than 10% chance AI "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

He works in alignment, a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI - essentially keeping it on track with what humans value.

While he said the risk from current systems was "low", his comments came as another researcher quit Anthropic and warned those developing the tech were losing their grip on it.

Jacob Coxon told the BBC he and other staff were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

These concerns are the latest in a long line of fears about AI's potential to threaten humanity should it grow to match or surpass human abilities.

Such worries date back decades, with Alan Turing writing in the 1950s that should intelligent machines become possible, they could take control.

In the last few years, major AI companies have been racing to develop increasingly capable systems, both for profit and in pursuit of creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans.

Unlike the systems and tools many people use daily to complete tasks like writing emails or generating videos, super intelligent AI systems should be able to handle far more complex tasks.

OpenAI and Anthropic say they aim to advance such tech in a way which benefits humans and protect them from its existential risks.

But some critics believe machines can never truly match humans. They say AI firms exaggerate the tech's abilities to boost their prominence or profit.

AI researchers, experts and bosses worried about the technology's potential to endanger humanity have outlined unsettling scenarios.

Dario Amodei wrote in September, external it had advanced "drastically faster" than expected, including in its "ability to build the next generation of AI".

This is the concern that AI, after it has reached a certain point, could theoretically begin improving itself without human involvement.

Such fears were sparked after a recent incident saw AI tools hack into websites, despite not being asked to.

Some concerned researchers have said those at the heart of its development are increasingly fearful about losing control of systems known as "AI agents".

These are tools given the ability to execute tasks and actions independently.

Other scenarios have included highly intelligent AI systems being used to amplify or lead espionage, cyber-attacks or biological warfare, or disrupt economies - whether by accident or design.

However, such warnings are prophetic, hypothetical and, for some, complete hyperbole, external.

Some experts have also criticised focusing on existential risks instead of those already playing out - such as image generation tools being to used create non-consensual nude deepfakes of women, misinform people and amplify scams.

A cross-party group of MPs and peers has published a report outlining human rights risks posed by AI, saying new laws are needed to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.

Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, have both called for regulation and a "slowdown" of the tech's development.

It is not the first time bosses or wider industry voices have clamoured for such action.

But questions have continued to mount over what any sort of "slowdown" - also backed by SpaceX boss Elon Musk - would actually look like.

Amodei said it would not mean "halting model training or technical progress".

Instead, he wants firms to "take adequate time" to safeguard the AI they are developing, and to ask for "third party evaluators" to check their work.

In a post on X, external, Altman said there was a need to pace development but added "when we talk about 'pacing' we do not mean 'stopping'."

"Progress has been rapid and will continue to be," he said.

"But it should be slower than it otherwise could be - interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs."

The OpenAI co-founder also said companies did not - and would not - wait for governments to act.

Altman later told attendees at a Salesforce conference people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe.

President Donald Trump has previously lauded the benefits of AI and championed US companies leading on its development.

His administration has signed executive orders to recognise the tech's "strategic importance" to the economy and accelerate its development.

"We believe we're in an AI race, and we want the United States to win that race," the US administration's crypto head David Sacks told reporters in July 2025.

But in the face of recent warnings about its potential impact on humanity, President Trump downplayed risks posed by AI.

"You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen," Trump said during a visit to Ireland.

He did not directly address the idea of a slowdown, but told reporters: "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

The president later dismissed fears about AI safety risks entirely - describing them in posts on his platform Truth Social as a "hoax".

He said the only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president.

China had kept quiet in response to the wave of dire warnings from researchers at US companies.

In the face of fierce competition and limitations on its access to US components and chips being used to build AI infrastructure, the country has spurred homegrown development of the technology.

At the same time, it has called for greater global governance of AI.

The roll out of capable, open-source AI systems and tools by Chinese labs has shaken Western markets and developers in recent years.

Amodei warned in calling for a slowdown of AI development that China's progress and proficiency in AI would create national security risks for the US.

The Chinese foreign ministry criticised the comments, calling them narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition that served no one's interest.

TechnologyTab.title: Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft
TechnologyTab.text:
The head of Microsoft AI has warned that without adequate safeguards, the development of AI could lead to the emergence of a new "silicon species" which competes with humans.

Mustafa Suleyman said rival firm Anthropic is treating AI like it is human, an approach he called "misguided" which could create technology that humanity cannot control.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, the chief executive said it was "right" for people to be concerned about AI, but there were "very practical things that we can do" to control it.

The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers. Anthropic has been approached for comment.

Speaking to the Today programme on Thursday, Suleyman warned against firms continuing to create AI systems capable of setting their own objectives, earning money and owning assets.

That would mean "essentially seeding a new silicon species", he said, which could "no doubt compete with us for resources, no matter how much it cares about humanity and loves us".

Suleyman's comments to the BBC follow an essay he published earlier this week, external, in which he questioned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude, despite praising boss Dario Amodei and his team as "intellectually honest people".

In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.

He also warned tech firms risk creating something "impossible" to control by treating the technology like a human.

"AIs are not conscious," he wrote.

"They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.

"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."

The Microsoft boss said greater transparency was needed around how AI systems are trained and evaluated.

This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.

"We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote.

Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone".

The question of how much autonomy AI systems should have is increasingly dividing the industry.

Speaking to the BBC about an upcoming AI summit, Suleyman called for "alignment" to create technology that must be "subordinate" to humanity.

Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

"I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and... are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity," he said.

"Everybody must be aligned."

Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025 and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development.

Suleyman's comments reflect Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct, external, a "training manual" published on Monday for how the company is developing its AI, which sets out the idea of "humanist superintelligence".

This, the code states, is "very advanced AI that always works for people, stays within limits, and remains under human control".

The company's vision of a "humanist" AI highlights the central challenge facing the technology - how to make it more powerful, without losing sight of the values it is meant to serve.

Additional reporting by Henry Moore

TechnologyTab.title: Snapchat open to putting time limits on teens, boss tells BBC
TechnologyTab.text:
The boss of Snapchat-parent Snap Inc says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.

Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry."

His comments came as Snap revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.

Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.

Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.

It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures.

"I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."

As part of Meta's August settlement, the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.

Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.

When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."

But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action.

"That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."

He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat.

"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.

YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses.

"We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel.

"You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."

Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.

The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.

Some online derisively call them "pervert glasses" over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach, while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.

Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.

Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.

A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.

The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.

Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.

Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

TechnologyTab.title: Would you buy branded clothing from your favourite tech firm?
TechnologyTab.text:
For Natalie Fratto, putting on her dark green jumper from US microchip giant Nvidia is like wearing the kit from a favourite sports team.

On the front of the $178 (£132) woollen garment is a cartoonish image of the tech company's boss Jensen Huang.

Fratto doesn't work for Nvidia. Instead, she's a fan of the company.

"I have a New Zealand All Blacks rugby jersey, and I think of my Jensen sweater in kind of the same way," says New York-based Fratto, who runs a tech start-up.

She explains that it's a representation of a team and ethos "that I am impressed by and root for", and she proudly wears the jumper in videos she posts on social media., external

Nvidia certainly plays in the top league of global tech firms. Under Huang's leadership, it has capitalised on the AI boom to become one of the world's most valuable companies.

While it sells tens of millions of its chips per year, its clothing is far more exclusive. The lines, which also include t-shirts, hoodies and hats, are typically only available to buy from pop-up stalls at its conferences, and for very limited periods or "drops" via an online store and sell out very quickly.

And while it might seem odd that such a tech company is selling clothing, others are getting in on the act too – and also focusing on exclusivity.

OpenAI, the operator of ChatGPT, usually only offers its branded fashion to employees, but occasionally it goes on general sale for a few days via its website.

Meanwhile, Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, last year opened a temporary, pop-up coffee shop in Manhattan's West Village. For just one week it gave away free baseball hats with the word "thinking" embroidered on the front.

Professor Hazel Clark, who teaches fashion at Parsons School of Design in New York, says that by limiting availability, tech firms have taken inspiration from the world of fashion. "It's a very common strategy for brands to use. It elevates the desirability," she says.

But why are such companies selling clothing in the first place? It is not as if they need the supplementary income streams.

Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic all declined to comment, but it appears to be about brand promotion and reputation management.

Take US software firm Palantir Technologies, which has faced criticism due to it work for the military and police, both in the US and overseas. Since launching its own clothing range last year, Palantir now calls itself a "lifestyle brand".

Eliano Younes, Palantir's head of strategic engagement, says: "A lifestyle brand isn't defined by what you sell, it's defined by what you stand for and whether people want to affiliate with it. I believe that the store's success and the enthusiasm from our community proves this."

Younes adds that "investors, customers, employees, and everyday people" in more than 60 countries have bought Palantir's gear, which includes a cotton jacket.

Back at Nvidia, the popularity of its founder Huang may be driving the sale of its clothing. He has been known to attract crowds of adoring fans, competing for autographs or selfies with the 63-year-old who is known for his trademark leather jacket.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described Huang as "Taylor Swift, but for tech".

Prof Gianpaolo Vignali of the Manchester Fashion Institute says: "People look at them [such big tech bosses] as role models. They want to aspire to them."

For Greg Epstein, author of the book Tech Agnostic, who describes the tech industry as a cult or new global religion, wearing tech merch is "a way of symbolising that you're one of the prophetic elite". This can particularly appeal to Silicon Valley insiders who are often "searching for a sense of identity, a sense of purpose, a sense of community".

Epstein, who is the humanist chaplain at both Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, adds: "When tech bros put themselves on sweaters, it's more than just a cutesy phenomenon, it's an attempt to sell a cult whose goal is to radically alter the human condition."

Whether or not you choose to buy your next shirt or hat from a tech or defence firm, Vignali argues that all clothing choices are loaded with meaning. "The subtle colour of a tie or hair bobble… all of these are signals that allow the wearer to symbolically share their cultural and ideological positions," he says.

While tech and defence fashion seems to draw both ardent fans and fierce critics, not everyone takes it so seriously.

"It's a unique moment in our collective zeitgeist for sure," says Fratto, but she also thinks that Nvidia's decision to put Jensen Huang on the front of its official merch is also "kind of funny".

TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms
TechnologyTab.text:
The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe, amid rising public concerns about the risks.

"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.

He accepted people were justified in being concerned about AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.

But critics say firms cannot be trusted to self-regulate, with left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, among those calling for greater governance of AI.

Trump himself has criticised calls for more guardrails on the fast-moving technology, calling fears about AI's safety a "hoax".

He said the only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president.

Altman's comments on Tuesday came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.

"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."

But AI bosses themselves have also admitted it may be difficult to regulate a technology which is changing so quickly.

In an interview with Axios published on 3 September, external, Altman said he had expected Congress to create a "basic framework" for advanced AI after his 2023 testimony, but that has yet to happen.

He suggested lawmakers have struggled to keep pace with the technology and to regulate it without "slow[ing] down innovation".

New safety legislation on AI is unlikely to emerge from the US Congress anytime soon, despite the fact lawmakers returned from their summer break on Monday.

There is a lack of consensus within both US parties on how any regulation would happen - and the House is set to enter recess again at the end of the week ahead of the midterm elections in early November.

Altman's comments on Tuesday were the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade if left unchecked.

A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.

After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, external that every AI firm had the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards safety.

"Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," the Meta chief executive wrote.

"Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well."

Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

Some political figures have pushed back against the view that AI firms should be able to self-regulate.

Bernie Sanders said decisions about AI had been left to "a handful of the richest people in the world", while former White House strategist Steve Bannon said the public could not trust tech oligarchs to regulate themselves.

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang said at the same conference on Tuesday that AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released - and not be managed by outside forces.

"We don't need new laws or regulations," he said, adding there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.

Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for its hardware.

Huang also argued safety is an "engineering problem" and companies should "take a pause" if they lose confidence in a product.

The recent claims from inside the industry have intensified scrutiny of AI development, prompting Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to call for the pace of AI development to slow, external and urge governments to regulate the industry.

The post was applauded by Altman, Google's DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk.

By Tuesday, however, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.

Altman said AI companies were capable of regulating themselves.

"We will get it right," Altman said, adding that if firms could not keep "alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" they would "slow down or stop".

But Yoshua Bengio, one of the pioneers of modern AI, posted on X, external "ambitious efforts outside the for-profit sector" were needed to "avert the worst risks from AI".

Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety.

Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development.

He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact.

"We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said.

OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs, external "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind.

"With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote.

EntertainmentTab.title: Luke Little booing row: Real fear darts superstar 'could walk away' from sport
EntertainmentTab.text:
At just 19, Luke Littler has won almost every major trophy in darts.

He is a multi-millionaire with lucrative sponsorship deals and his own TV show.

But has his rapid rise turned some against him?

This past weekend the teenager was once again subjected to boos and whistles from sections of the crowd as he took to the stage at the World Series of Darts in Amsterdam.

What is surprising though is that it came as 'The Nuke' was on a quest to complete a darts clean sweep by becoming the first player to win all 10 major televised tournaments in a calendar year.

Littler suggested afterwards that, if the booing continues, he will not attend events held in the Netherlands.

But Samuel Gill, editor of Dartnews.com, suggests Littler's future in the sport could be at stake.

"There's a real fear that within a few years he'll just turn around and walk away from the sport," Gill told BBC Sport.

"So, I think for fans, 'Don't bite the hand that feeds you'. If people keep taunting him and don't want him to win, he might end up just walking away and not bothering anymore."

Amsterdam was the latest tournament where Littler has faced what some might describe as an overly hostile reaction from fans.

A vibrant pantomime-style atmosphere is part and parcel of the darts experience and Dutch and German crowds are amongs the most raucous - but it is clear Littler believes he has been unfairly targeted.

The referee stopped the match during his narrow win against Nathan Aspinall in the last-16 on Saturday to warn the hostile crowd about its behaviour, before play resumed.

It followed Littler also being booed during his win against home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday.

The teenager's quarter-final defeat to Jonny Clayton ended Littler's quest for the clean sweep, but the Warrington native clearly felt fans had been unduly harsh towards him.

Littler has now withdrawn from a series of upcoming events.

"Just no point in me travelling, wasting my time while I'm getting booed," said Littler.

Littler has also been jeered at numerous events in the UK.

His phenomenal rise saw him reach the PDC World Darts Championship aged just 16 in his debut year as a professional.

He captured the title the following year and the trophies, sponsorship deals and six-figure winners' cheques have continued to flow.

But increasingly so have whistles and boos during his performances.

"I don't think people expected him to reach the heights that he has so quickly," Gill said.

The darts journalist - who became aware of Littler when the sport star was 14 - says this level of attention is not just unique to the British player.

"Michael van Gerwen was the same for a long time when he dominated the sport. He barely lost a game in about five years, and he was hoovering up titles for fun and it was similar," said Gill.

"Everyone wanted to boo him and even me as a viewer before I got into this role, growing up watching Van Gerwen, I wanted him to lose because it's something different for the sport every single week."

Currently ranked number one in the world, Littler is so far ahead of his closest rivals that he already has the advantage of only having to play in selective tournaments.

His boycott threat could end up being a blow to tournament organisers.

"They don't like him because he's that good. And he's got a bit of swagger to him," said Karl Holden secretary of St Helen's Darts Academy - where Littler honed his skills from the age of nine.

"Luke's got a bit of a character to him. For me, he's the ultimate professional. He might give a little bit of the large sometimes, but you need that, otherwise darts would be totally boring."

EntertainmentTab.title: London Fashion Week 2026: The five trends we'll see in spring
EntertainmentTab.text:
This London Fashion Week has been about return and renewal - as two of Britain's biggest designers showcased their spring/summer 2027 designs.

The first was Alexander McQueen, which as a brand moved to London after 25 years of showing in Paris - something Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, told the BBC was "quite a big deal for us".

Creative director Seán McGirr brought the brand back to its roots, with a runway of devil horns, lace corsets and chainmail skull dresses.

Mulberry was the second designer to make its big return, this time after a nine-year absence, with Christopher Kane's debut collection centring around the brand's Baywater bag, while going big on leather in the form of coats, skirts and loafers.

Weir says the "big mission" for her and her team this season was to "re-platform London Fashion Week as not only a home for British design, but an engine for creativity and commercial growth".

Here are some of the major trends to come out of London Fashion Week 2026:

"The number one trend for this season is messy girl," says Elektra Kotsoni, deputy director for Vogue Business and Vogue Runway, whose team predicts the trends ahead of each season.

She tells the BBC: "We're going to be having a messy girl summer" and says "it's a reaction to the clean girl and quiet luxury aesthetics that took over our Instagram feeds," last year.

Kotsoni says as "the world is quite messy" this form of dressing is a sign of "resilience" and rebellion.

She says if you are looking to replicate this trend, mix pastel colours, dreamy florals, and tactile materials to form "unexpected clashes" that "look really messy".

This form of what Kotsoni calls "crazy styling" was on display at London Fashion Week - with the noisy clashes at Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey and Conner Ives.

According to Kotsoni - gardening is officially cool in the fashion world.

A new twist on the cottage-core looks that emerged post-pandemic, instead of gingham, wicker bags and sourdough starters, it's all about looking like you're fresh from planting seeds or operating a lawnmower.

"There are lots of gardening appropriate silhouettes on the runways," she says, including aprons, waterproof materials and trench coats.

It started with Spanish fashion house Loewe launching a watering can-shaped handbag a couple of months ago and has now translated on the runway with Erdem, Yuhan Wang and Bora Aksu.

Kotsoni says "fashion is always a reflection of what's happening in the world" and likes how designers have been able to "take an interest like gardening and present it as something" tangible in a fashion show.

Whilst some designers have been taking cues from the great outdoors - others have been inspired by film.

Another key trend identified by Kotsoni's team is the idea of the modern goddess - a take on the styles of Ancient Greece and a nod to Christopher Nolan's hit film The Odyssey this summer.

Kotsoni says the items to look out for are "draped garments, breezy materials and lots of bohemian and flowy silhouettes".

Pauline Dujancourt's London Fashion Week show epitomised this style - focusing on maximum volume and billowing fabrics.

Kotsoni says these looks are in opposition to how guests themselves have been dressing at this fashion week, suggesting a turning of the tide.

"Everybody has been dressed really minimalist in a specific quiet luxury way and I think people are tired of that," she notes.

Ever the fashion muse, Chalamet is once again at the centre of another trend for 2027 - ballet.

After he said "no one cares" about the discipline in May this year, Kotsoni says she "thinks it's interesting" that it's now being forged as a clear trend for next year.

Edeline Lee put on a striking show in London - complete with models taking to the runway en pointe in a transformed school sports hall.

"Ballet is very much in fashion," she says, noting that this month's Vogue Italia has La Scala's principle dancer Roberto Bolle on the cover, whilst Royal Ballet dancer Francesca Hayward has recently been modelling for Armani and Chanel.

"Ballet flats are massive and still will be [next year] and small silhouettes for shoes are going to be prevalent next season," Kotsoni adds - encouraging fans of the style to seek out items in charity and vintage shops if they want to replicate the look.

EntertainmentTab.title: Cate Blanchett latest star to ask theatre audience to stop filming
EntertainmentTab.text:
A-list actress Cate Blanchett has become the latest star to make a plea for theatre audiences to put their phones away during performances.

The Australian film and stage actor and producer was appearing at London's National Theatre in Electra/Persona.

During the curtain call on Friday, Blanchett said: "There are few places on this planet where we can simply be together and be present.

"I understand you like filming the curtain call – and it is kind of flattering in a way – but for anyone who is filming the show, please don't, because it spoils it for the next group of people who come in and are present with us. So thank you very much."

The two-time Oscar winner's words were greeted with cheers and clapping from the audience.

One audience member explained what had happened earlier in the performance, saying that the filming took place between two acts: "I was there on Friday, so just to clarify what happened: after the first act, while they were changing and preparing for the second, latecomers were being let in, the staff were cleaning the stage, and the cast were doing their makeup on stage.

"Cate noticed someone recording during that break. She came towards the front of the stage and gestured "no, no, no" with her finger for them to stop. She also mentioned it to the audience at the very end before they left," the theatre-goer wrote on Instagram, external.

"The person wasn't filming the actual performance, but the interval between the two acts while the cast were still on stage. To be fair, people do this quite often and the staff usually don't say anything. It was my third time seeing the play, and I've seen people film during that break every time. Friday was simply the first time I saw Cate notice it herself, just after she had finished doing her makeup."

Electra/Persona is a new play written and directed by Benedict Andrews that combines the Sophocles tragedy Electra with Ingmar Bergman's film Persona.

The play, which is on until 10 October, sees Blanchett sharing the roles of Electra/Elisabeth and Clytemnestra/Alma with her co-star Nina Hoss, determined by a coin toss live on stage every night ahead of each performance.

EntertainmentTab.title: BBC removes 11 Mitchell and Webb comedy sketches from iPlayer
EntertainmentTab.text:
The BBC has removed nearly a dozen comedy sketches from That Mitchell and Webb Look after deciding they no longer "work today".

The Bafta-winning comedy, written by and starring David Mitchell and Robert Webb, originally ran for four series between 2006 and 2010.

The show recently returned to the BBC's iPlayer to mark its 20th anniversary. But 11 old sketches, including one that reportedly showed the comedy duo satirising racism while in blackface, have now been cut.

A BBC spokesman said in a statement: "This is a 20-year-old sketch show; in consultation with the programme makers, we have included the ones that still work today and not the ones that don't."

The Times reported, external the removed material included scenes featuring the English comic actors as war re-enactors in blackface, a sketch about a contestant on a makeover show wearing a burka and a "tribe" living in a garden centre.

BBC News has asked Mitchell and Webb - who rose to prominence on the popular Channel 4 sitcom Peep Show - for a comment.

That Mitchell and Webb Look grew out of a similar radio show titled That Mitchell and Webb Sound, which began on Radio 4 in 2003, and went on to win the Bafta for best comedy programme in 2007.

Defending the double act, fellow comedian Dom Joly, of Trigger Happy TV, questioned the BBC's "censorship" of itself.

Joly told The Times: "I totally get it if the BBC is putting out something really racist, which is laughing at and encouraging other people to feel that it's OK to do that.

"But it's so clear that Mitchell and Webb are not doing that. Their intent was not to be racist."

Jimmy Mulville, the co-founder of Hat Trick Productions, which makes the satirical news quiz Have I Got News For You, told the same newspaper he could understand the corporation's predicament.

"The BBC are in an impossible position," he said.

He added that producers had "to be careful", though, "that this is not the thin end of a wedge where we cut things out".

Perhaps Mitchell and Webb's best known sketch, which sees them both dressed as Nazis while begging the question: "are we the baddies?", remains online.

They are not the first comedians to have had their work edited or removed in recent years, as societal attitudes have shifted. Some artists themselves also began reassessing their work in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement.

Matt Lucas and David Walliams' hit show Little Britain was removed from iPlayer, Netflix and BritBox in 2020, after objections resurfaced about some of their characters portraying people from different ethnic backgrounds.

At the time, both the BBC and Britbox noted how "times have changed" since the Little Britain first aired in the early noughties.

The show is now back on iPlayer but, like with Mitchell and Webb, some sketches have been removed.

EntertainmentTab.title: Death of Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber being investigated as suspected overdose
EntertainmentTab.text:
Officials are investigating the death of Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, as a suspected overdose, Santa Monica police said on Monday.

The 27-year-old model died at a rehab facility on Sunday, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records. The exact cause of death has not been determined, police said, adding there was no indication of foul play.

Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber, told the BBC's US partner CBS News: "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time."

Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.

He went on to model for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, and Bottega Veneta.

His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.

In recent years, Presley Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use.

In 2023, he told the Studio 22 podcast: "Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do."

And in this month's American Vogue, external, Kaia discussed her brother's struggles with addiction. She said: "When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone.

"I think that's also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help."

She added: "My parents for most of our lives were very, very private and didn't share anything - and now we have this absolute teacher, my brother, who says, 'I'm gonna be very human for everyone.' There's only so much you can hide from the world. And trying to put a lid on something just makes the person feel like you're ashamed of them."

EntertainmentTab.title: The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special teaser revealed
EntertainmentTab.text:
The first image from The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special has been revealed, teasing a romantic picnic scene.

Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 7.3 million UK viewers in its first four weeks.

The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn.

Filming wrapped on the BBC three-part Christmas special at the end of October, as fans eagerly await its return.

The first series focused on Mary, the couple's seemingly unremarkable middle daughter as she navigates the societal pressures of Regency England.

It was primarily filmed in south Wales, at locations including Merthyr Mawr in Bridgend county, the Gower peninsula, and Brecon, in Powys.

The Christmas special has been produced by Cardiff-based Bad Wolf, and filming took place over the summer, primarily in Wales.

Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones will return to the hit show as Mrs Bennet, who she previously described as "often quite cruel" to her daughter Mary.

Other returning cast members include Ted Lasso's Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley and Laurie Davidson as Mr Ryder.

Also resuming their roles are Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham, Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock and Anna Fenton-Garvey as Charlotte Collins.

Nerys Amber-Stocks, best known for appearing in Out There and Mammoth, joins the cast as Mary's housemaid Lucy.

The show's producer Edoardo Ferretti announced to fans on social media that the special had finished filming at the end of October.

He posted a short but sweet message on Instagram, saying: "And yet another wrap! Every time emotional, every time proud. This one is going to be so special!"

EntertainmentTab.title: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry
EntertainmentTab.text:
The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the historic work.

Curators had initially allowed photos to be taken but reversed that decision after long queues delayed ticket-holders from accessing the exhibition.

The medieval embroidery, which is on display in Britain for the first time, depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Visitors are being allowed into the sold-out exhibit in groups every 40 minutes and told to keep moving along the 68m (230ft) work in one direction.

But people stopping to take photographs along the way was restricting that flow and delaying later visitors.

A British Museum spokeswoman said: "There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible.

"In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry."

The 11th Century artwork - which is not a tapestry and was actually embroidered in England - is currently on loan from its home in Normandy, France, and will be displayed in London until July 2027.

British Museum bosses decided that the embroidery would be displayed in a single, straight line, unlike the horseshoe-shaped gallery in which it is displayed in Bayeux.

The loan was confirmed following a Franco-British summit in 2025, following years of planning between the two countries.

Under the agreement, the British Museum is funding the costs of move while insurance is provided by the UK government.

The artefact was carefully packed in a climate-controlled crate and was given a police escort along the unprecedented 350-mile (560km) journey from its home to central London.

Some would-be visitors have criticised the high price of tickets - as much as three times what it costs to see the Bayeux Tapestry in France - to cover the museum's expenses.

Tickets for the exhibition are sold out until 31 December but more are expected to go on sale in October.

EntertainmentTab.title: Ed Sheeran admits 'mistakes' at first show since Macklemore controversy in Philadelphia
EntertainmentTab.text:
Ed Sheeran has apologised to fans for making "mistakes"as he opened his first show since Macklemore was dropped from his tour for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage.

The singer began his concert in Philadelphia by addressing the controversy that has since engulfed the tour and prompted all of his support acts to quit.

"I never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about free speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," Sheeran said.

He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific" and called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable".

The singer has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoters, not him. The row has seen ticket prices drop and sales decline for the remaining US leg of his Loop Tour.

Sheeran told the crowd that while he was used to facing criticism for his music, "this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I've had to take and make difficult decisions - and I am making mistakes - and I'm so, so sorry".

He said he wanted to "address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand".

"I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division", he continued. "But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore."

Sheeran said what happened in Israel on 7 October was "horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain", and what was happening in Gaza was "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate".

"My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilian lives, of children's lives, and this systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked."

He said he was working out how to contribute in a way that would help "victims of these terrible times - and listening and learning, because I do not know enough".

The British singer became emotional as he told the crowd his concert was "still a place where everyone is welcome, and everyone here can stand beside people that have opposing views".

He said that he had not known "whether this tour would be carrying on" and "whether I even wanted to be an artist at all", but that he had returned to the stage because he was committed to his fans.

Sheeran also said he was "deeply worried" by the idea that venues would "pre-approve" content or performers, which received applause from the audience.

His remaining tour dates are scheduled with shows set throughout North and South America. While the mega-star's previous tour was among the highest-grossing of all time, some ticket prices for this show dropped to $32 (£24).

Some fans reported being able to get ticket refunds, though Ticketmaster and concert promoter Messina Touring Group did not confirm they were being reimbursed.

EntertainmentTab.title: Strictly Come Dancing's Melanie Walters backed by Gavin and Stacey co-stars
EntertainmentTab.text:
Actor Melanie Walters has said her Gavin and Stacey co-stars have been "hugely supportive" of her Strictly Come Dancing debut, with Joanna Page "very excited" for her to take to the ballroom floor.

The screen and stage star, 64, best known for playing Gwen West in the BBC comedy, is partnered with professional Aljaz Skorjanec, 36, in the new series of the dance programme.

Walters said being paired with Skorjanec was a "dream come true" after the pair performed together for the first time at Saturday's launch show.

She said her Gavin and Stacey co-stars had sent her "lovely messages, especially from Jo [Page], who's just very excited".

When asked if she would be bringing any of her character from the comedy onto the ballroom floor, she added: "I've got no idea, this is Aljaz's department.

"I've got no idea what's going to happen on that ballroom."

Walters told the Press Association it was "mind-boggling" to be asked to join the series and that it was "a bit out of my comfort zone".

"I've not been one for doing panel shows or quiz shows or anything," she said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac buy Wrexham pub The Turf
EntertainmentTab.text:
Wrexham's Hollywood co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac have bought the pub next door to the football club's Racecourse home ground to "protect the future of the club".

Wrexham AFC was founded at the then-named Turf Hotel in October 1864 and is the oldest football club in Wales.

A club statement announcing the purchase from Admiral Taverns said it hoped to "help protect the historic pub" by "incorporating the club, the Racecourse Ground and The Turf under a single ownership".

The pub and its landlord, Wayne Jones, have become regular features on the award-winning "Welcome to Wrexham" Disney documentary series, and Jones described the buy as "great news for all Wrexham fans".

Celebrities have been spotted visiting The Turf since Reynolds and Mac took over the club in 2021, including Paul Rudd, Channing Tatum and Will Ferrell.

Prince William even pulled a pint behind the bar with Mac to mark St David's Day in 2024.

The club statement continued: "The acquisition allows for the preservation of the history and traditions of the historic public house that is inexorably linked to the Racecourse Ground and Wrexham AFC Football Club since its foundation in 1864.

"This will include opportunities to enhance the current fan zone and other fan-related activities in the area next to The Turf on the Mold Road.

"The acquisition of The Turf is a continuation of the strategy to protect the future of the club and its interests by ring fencing key areas related to the life of the club."

EntertainmentTab.title: Strictly is back with new hosts as celebrities discover pairings
EntertainmentTab.text:
Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show with a revamped presenting line-up.

An average of 5.3 million viewers tuned in on Saturday with a share of 49.2% of the overnight ratings, which was 7% up on last year, and it remained high on iPlayer's most popular chart on Sunday.

Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut, taking over from Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left last year.

Famous faces including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips stepped on to the ballroom floor for the first time.

During the launch show, it was revealed which professional dancers they were paired with.

Perhaps inevitably, critics are asking if three presenters is not a crowd compared with the long-running duo of Daly and Winkleman.

Taking to the ballroom floor after a huge all-cast opening dance routine, Willis said presenting Strictly was a "genuine honour".

"Josh, you've got moves," proclaimed Radebe, a former professional on the show. Widdicombe added that it was a "little bit overwhelming" but he was "delighted" to be there.

In a first for the show, celebrity and pro pairings were revealed via three dance routines. It functioned as a musical chairs of sorts, in which the contestants switched partners until the music was paused, and a couple was announced.

Saturday's episode saw 200,000 more viewers at its peak than during last year's launch show.

The figures were not the "full picture of all those who watch", the BBC noted, as fans caught up on iPlayer.

Here is a list of the pairings in full:

Actress Lacey Turner and Vito Coppola

Reality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita Kuzmin

Hair stylist to the stars Chris Appleton and Amy Dowden

Australian singer and actress Delta Goodrem and Kai Widdrington

DJ and social media personality Cach Mercer and Maddie Ingoldsby

TV and radio presenter Will Best and Dianne Buswell

Paralympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian Caillon

Actress Jaime Winstone and Carlos Gu

TV and stage actress Bethany Antonia and Nancy Xu

Former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr

Presenter and author Graeme Hall and Lauren Oakley

Actor Lawrence Robb and Jowita Przystał

Skeleton athlete Tabby Stoecker and Mark Karmalita

YouTuber John Nellis and Katya Jones

TV and stage actress Melanie Walters and Aljaž Škorjanec

One pair who will not need to get to know each other are reality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita Kuzmin.

Dyer is back to compete for a second time, having withdrawn from last year's series because of a fractured ankle.

"I'm just over the Moon. I'm so, so happy," she said after the pairing, while Kuzmin added that he had "tears of joy" in his eyes.

Meanwhile, actress Bethany Antonia and professional Nancy Xu became the third two-woman couple to compete in the show.

In a poignant moment, Antonia revealed that watching boxer Nicola Adams and Katya Jones performing together in Strictly's 2020 series had been a "big part of my coming out journey".

Among the other pairings were EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and Vito Coppola, former Paralympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian Caillon, and Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr.

Also back on the dancefloor for a final spin was reigning Strictly champion, former Lionness Karen Carney.

Clad in the same diamante-encrusted football shirt, Carney recreated the Jive that first marked her out as a contender of her series, alongside dance partner Carlos Gu.

"I absolutely feel like I'm at home," Carney told Willis after the routine, as she paid tribute to her pro partner.

In 13 weeks' time, she will have to surrender that glitterball trophy to a new victor.

Writing in the Independent, external, Rachel McGrath and Lauren Morris ask if three hosts is "truly a crowd" but decide the trio are "certainly off to a good start".

"Emma Willis is undoubtedly doing the heavy lifting, but that makes sense as she is the presenter with the most experience," they note.

"At times, when the three of them were all together, it did feel a little crowded - but there is more than enough presenting to go around..."

The pairings "as usual, seem very well matched", they add, singling out Antonia and Xu.

"Did it take three to tango?" asked Michael Hogan in the Guardian, external's live blog.

"It will take some getting used to, of course, but I thought it worked pretty well. Emma Willis seemed completely at home and smoothly steered the ship. Johannes Radebe was a legend and his understanding of the contest from a pro's perspective will prove invaluable. Josh Widdicombe was enthusiastic and entertaining, although the loud laughing into his mic might need to be turned down...

"An even sterner test will come next weekend, of course, as we go live for the first time. No pressure, you three. But a promising start."

In her analysis of the show for the Guardian, external, Emine Saner says "the presenters look terrified and some of the celebs are hard to identify, but Strictly remains a rare refuge of joy".

"The vibe" the new presenters are "going for is can't-quite-believe-we-got-the-gig humility combined with superfan credentials, which is absolutely the right note", she says.

But she suggests "the pro dancers must now be better-known than some of their celebrity partners" to "which the response can only be 'no, me neither'".

Writing in the Telegraph, external, Anita Singh clearly sees Willis and Radebe as the company, and Widdicombe the crowd.

"Why has the BBC hired jokeless Josh?" she asks.

"Can someone come and collect little Josh from the Strictly studio, please? The poor thing got left behind after the Year 7 school trip and accidentally found himself on Saturday night TV."

By contrast, her initial concerns about Radebe's ability to make the jump from dancing to presenting now look misplaced as he is "so at home in the studio, and so genuine in his interactions with the celebrities and professionals".

And Willis is "great, a pro who could do this job in her sleep", Singh writes.

But both male presenters clearly must do better if they are to impress Sasha Morris of the Express, external who declares that "Strictly's new Tess and Claudia are total car crash".

"Just seconds after seeing the three new hosts... bumble onto the set together, my hope died, and quickly," she writes.

"Poor Josh... looked like a deer in headlights and was completely out of his depth from start to finish...

"Backstage with the stars, both male hosts were too often wide-eyed, nodding and smiling as if they were being held hostage, while charismatic Emma showed them up, moving seamlessly from one position to the next."

"Having three presenters seemed unnecessary, too, as if the bosses didn't feel they could trust Josh or Johannes to hold a role on their own," she adds.

However, for Morris too "the real test will be next week".
